lines.text: Pyramids were high on his list of favorite things.
He didn’t have to worry about being eaten by a pyramid.
In case we want to come right back here.”
Annie found the book with the picture of their hometown in it.
Then Jack pointed to the pyramid picture in the Egypt book.
He cleared his throat and said, “I wish we could go to this place.”
Jack looked out the tree house window.
A black cat was perched on a branch.
The cat was staring at Jack and Annie.
It was the strangest cat Jack had ever seen.
He was very sleek and dark.
“It’s the cat in the Egypt book,” whispered Annie.
Just then the wind started to blow.
Jack closed his eyes as the tree house started to spin.
Hot bright sunlight nearly blinded him.
Jack and Annie looked out the window.
The tree house was perched on the top of a palm tree.
The tree stood with other palm trees.
A patch of green surrounded by a sandy desert.
The black cat was sitting at the base of the tree.
His yellow eyes were staring up at Jack and Annie.
The black cat stood and began walking around the tree.
She leaned out the window to see where the cat was going.
Jack leaned forward and looked down.
The cat was running away from the palm trees.
Toward a giant pyramid in the desert.
A parade was going toward the pyramid.
The same parade as in the Egypt book.
Jack looked down at the Egypt book.
He read the words under the picture: When a royal person died, a grand funeral procession took place.
Family, servants, and mourners followed the coffin.
The coffin was called a sarcophagus.
It was pulled on a sled by four oxen.
“The box is called a sar … sar … sar … oh, forget it.”
She started down the rope ladder.
Jack looked up from his notebook.
“There’s probably a mummy in that gold box,” Annie called up.
She sure knew how to get to him.
Jack shoved his notebook and the Egypt book into his pack.
Then he started down the ladder.
When he got to the ground, he and Annie took off across the sand.
But as they ran a strange thing happened.
The closer they got to the parade, the harder it was to see it.
But the great stone pyramid was still there.
There’s no such thing as ghosts,” said Jack.
It happens in the desert all the time,” said Jack.
But it just turns out to be the sunlight reflecting through heat.”
“How could sunlight look like people, a mummy box, and a bunch of cows?”
Near the base was the sleek black cat.
He was staring at Jack and Annie.
The cat started to slink away.
He walked along the base of the pyramid and slid around a corner.
They dashed around the corner—just in time to see the cat disappear through a hole in the pyramid.
He and Annie peeked through the hole.
He pulled out the Egypt book and turned to the section on pyramids.
He read the caption aloud: Pyramids were sometimes called Houses of the Dead.
They were nearly all solid stone, except for the burial chambers deep inside.
To the burial chambers,” said Annie.
Then he stepped out of the hot, bright sunlight into the cool, dark pyramid.
The floor slanted up from where they stood.
“We have to go farther inside,” said Annie.
She gave him a little push.
Jack started up the slanting floor of the hallway.
The hallway went on and on.
“I want to look at the book.”
He opened the Egypt book again.
He held it below a torch on the wall.
The book showed a picture of the inside of the pyramid.
“The burial chamber is in the middle of the pyramid.
Jack tucked the book under his arm.
Then they headed deeper into the pyramid.
“I think we’re almost at the burial chamber.
Then you come to the chamber.
A strange cry shot through the pyramid.
Out of the shadows flew a white figure.
The white figure moved swiftly past them.
He picked up the Egypt book.
She lifted something from the floor.
A dog’s head was carved on one end.
“It looks like a scepter,” said Jack.
“It’s a thing kings and queens carry,” said Jack.
“It means they have power over the people.”
“But the mummy—” “That was no mummy,” said Jack.
“What kind of person would be inside a pyramid?”
At last he found a picture of a person in a pyramid.
He read: Tomb robbers often carried off the treasure buried with mummies.
False passages were sometimes built to stop the robbers.
“Yeah, a robber who steals stuff from tombs.”
“But what if the robber comes back,” said Annie.
“But first I want to write something down.”
He put the Egypt book into his pack.
He pulled out his notebook and pencil.
He started writing in his notebook: “Jack—” said Annie.
Jack felt a whoosh of cold air.
A wave of terror went through him.
Another figure was moving slowly toward them.
She wore flowers in her black hair.
Her long white dress had many tiny pleats.
She handed him the gold scepter.
The lady stopped in front of them.
The scepter passed right through the lady’s hand.
But Jack could only stare in horror.
She spoke in a hollow, echoing voice.
Is it true that you have come to help me?”
“For a thousand years,” said the ghost-queen, “I have waited for help.”
Jack’s heart was pounding so hard he thought he might faint.
“Someone must find my Book of the Dead,” she said.
“I need it to go on to the Next Life.”
“Why do you need the Book of the Dead?”
She didn’t sound scared at all.
“It will tell me the magic spells I need to get through the Underworld,” said the ghost-queen.
“Before I journey on to the Next Life, I must pass through the horrors of the Underworld.”
“My brother hid the Book of the Dead.
So tomb robbers would not steal it,” said the ghost-queen.
“Then he carved this secret message on the wall, telling me how to find it.”
“Alas, my brother forgot my strange problem.
I cannot see clearly that which is close to my eyes.
I have not been able to read his message for a thousand years.”
“Oh, that’s not a strange problem,” said Annie.
The ghost-queen stared in wonder at Jack.
“Jack, lend her your glasses,” said Annie.
Jack took his glasses off his nose.
He held them out to the ghost-queen.
“I fear I cannot wear your glasses, Jack,” she said.
“But perhaps you will describe the hieroglyphs on these walls,” said the ghost-queen.
said Jack, finally finding his voice.
“It’s the ancient Egyptian way of writing.
Then he stepped toward the wall and took a good long look.
Jack and Annie squinted at the pyramid wall.
A series of tiny pictures were carved into the stone.
“There are four pictures here,” Jack told the ghostqueen.
One at a time, please,” she said.
He made a zigzag in the air with his finger.
“The second one has a long box on the bottom,” he said.
He drew it in the air.
She drew squiggly lines in the air.
More like a boat,” said Annie.
Jack took another look at the wall.
It could be a boat,” he said.
Jack and Annie studied the next picture.
“The third one is like a thing that holds flowers,” said Annie.
“Or a thing that holds water,” said Jack.
Jack and Annie studied the last picture.
“And the last one looks like a pole that droops,” said Annie.
“But one side is shorter than the other.”
Jack put down the scepter and got out his pencil.
“But that is the hieroglyph for a folded cloth,” said the ghost-queen.
He looked at the fourth hieroglyph again.
He still couldn’t see the folded cloth.
Unless it was like a towel hanging over a bathroom rod.
“So that’s all of them,” said Annie.
Jack wrote the words in his notebook.
Jack put the scepter and his notebook and pencil into his pack.
He and Annie followed the ghost-queen.
Until they came to some stairs.
The ghost-queen floated up the stairs.
The ghost-queen floated right through a wooden door.
Jack and Annie pushed on the door.
They stepped into a cold, drafty room.
The ghost-queen was nowhere in sight.
Dim torchlight lit the huge room.
It had a very high ceiling.
On one side was a pile of tables, chairs, and musical instruments.
On the other side of the room was a small wooden boat.
“What’s it doing inside Queen Hutepi’s pyramid?”
“Maybe it’s supposed to carry her to the Next Life,” said Jack.
He and Annie went over to the boat.
The boat was filled with many things.
He reached into the boat and lifted out a clay jug.
Jack felt down inside the jug.
“It feels like a big napkin,” he said.
Jack reached into the jug and pulled out the folded cloth.
It was wrapped around an ancient-looking scroll.
It was covered with wonderful hieroglyphs.
Jack traced his finger over the scroll.
It felt like very old paper.
We found your Book of the Dead!”
Then another door on the other side of the chamber creaked open.
Cold air was coming through the open doorway.
“She’s waited a thousand years for her book.
Jack put the ancient scroll into his backpack.
Then he and Annie slowly started to cross the drafty room.
They came to the open door.
Jack stepped into the other room.
Except for a long gold box.
The cover was on the floor.
There was still no sign of the ghost-queen.
“Let’s leave the scroll on the floor.
I think we should leave it in there,” said Annie.
She pointed to the gold box.
Annie took Jack by the arm.
They stopped in front of the box.
Bandages were still wrapped around the bald skull.
But most of the bandages had come off the face.
Plus the rotting bandages on her body were coming off.
She started out of the room.
She was standing by the door.
Jack pulled out the Egypt book and flipped to a picture of a mummy.
He read aloud: Ancient Egyptians tried to protect the body so it would last forever.
First it was dried out with salt.
He kept reading: Next it was covered with oil.
Then it was wrapped tightly in bandages.
She dashed out of the room.
“We have to give her the Book of the Dead!”
He pulled out the scroll and the scepter.
He put them next to the mummy’s skull.
Or did a deep sigh seem to shudder throughout the room?
Did the mummy’s face grow calmer?
Jack held his breath as he backed away.
At the bottom of the stairs, he heaved his own sigh.
Where in the world was Annie?
Had she run out of the pyramid?
He was running away from her voice.
He went back toward the burial chambers.
He went back into the boat room.
Right next to the door he had just come through.
He found himself at the top of some stairs.
They were just like the stairs in the other hallway.
He went down into the hallway.
It was lit by torches on the wall.
It was just like the other hallway.
She was running through the hallway toward him.
“I think this is one of those false passages.
Built to fool the tomb robbers,” said Jack.
“Yeah, it looks just like the right hallway,” said Jack.
“We have to go back into the boat room.
Just then they heard a creaking noise.
Then they watched in horror as the door slowly creaked shut.
A deep sound rumbled in the distance.
And all the torches went out.
“We have to get out of here fast.
“Good idea,” said Annie in a small voice.
They felt their way through the darkness.
To the top of the stairs.
Everything’s going to be okay,” said Jack.
He was trying to stay calm.
They leaned against the wooden door and pushed.
It was getting harder to breathe.
“Just … just rest a moment,” said Jack, panting.
His heart was pounding as he tried to see through the darkness.
“Maybe we should start down the hall,” he said.
“Maybe we’ll eventually come to … to an exit.”
Jack felt the stone wall as he climbed slowly down the stairs.
Jack started down the dark hallway.
It was impossible to see anything.
Taking one step at a time.
Moving his hands along the wall.
Was this the same door they had started at?
Annie took his hand in the dark.
They stood together at the top of the stairs.
They started down the dark hallway.
Hands against the wall, Jack and Annie stumbled through the darkness.
All the way through the winding hallway.
And another … Finally they saw a light at the end of the tunnel.
They rushed forward—out into the bright sunlight.
“How did we get out of the false passage?”
“But how could the cat do it?”
Then he disappeared in the shimmering waves of heat.
Jack looked toward the palm trees.
At the top of one sat the tree house.
He and Annie set off for the palm trees.
It was a long hot walk back.
At last Annie grabbed onto the rope ladder.
Once they were inside the tree house, Jack reached for the book about Pennsylvania.
Just then he heard a rumbling sound.
The same sound they had heard in the pyramid.
Annie said, pointing out the window.
A boat was beside the pyramid.
It was gliding over the sand.
Like a boat sailing over the sea.
Or was the ghost-queen finally on her way to the Next Life?
He pointed to the picture of Frog Creek.
“I wish we could go home,” he said.
The tree house started to spin.
Late-morning sunlight shone through the tree house window.
Shadows danced on the walls and ceiling.
He was lying on the floor of the tree house.
“I wonder what Mom’s making for lunch,” said Annie.
She was looking out the window.
“I hope it’s peanut butter and jelly sandwiches,” he said.
“Boy, this place is a mess,” said Annie.
Jack had almost forgotten about M.
Would they ever meet the mysterious M?
The person who seemed to own all the books in the tree house?
“Let’s put the Egypt book on the bottom of the pile,” said Annie.
He needed a rest before he visited any more ancient tombs.
“Let’s put the dinosaur book on top of the Egypt book,” said Annie.
And a long rest before he visited another Tyrannosaurus rex.
“The castle book can go on the very top of the pile,” said Annie.
He liked thinking about the knight on the cover of the castle book.
He felt as if the knight were his friend.
She was pointing at the wooden floor.
Jack groaned as he got up.
He stood next to Annie and looked at the floor.
“Turn your head a little,” said Annie.
“You have to catch the light just right.”
Jack tipped his head to one side.
Something was shining on the floor.
He tipped his head a bit more.
This proved the tree house belonged to M.
Jack touched the M with his finger.
Then he and Annie climbed down the ladder.
As they stood on the ground below the tree house, Jack heard a sound in the bushes.
“I’m going to bring the medallion back soon,” Jack said loudly.
“I feel like M is nearby,” Jack whispered.
But just then their mother’s voice came from the distance.
Jack and Annie looked around at the trees.
Then they looked at each other.
And they took off, running out of the woods.
They ran right into their mom.
She was making peanut butter and jelly sandwiches.
